open_obligations: Check whether Wu et al.'s decomposition in their book experiments is fixed rather than chosen by H or a model.
Check that Wu et al. train with RL from human feedback, not only supervised distillation.
Check whether leaf tasks are evaluated by humans in place of H's composition step.
Check that Wu et al. cite Christiano et al. as a source for their task decomposition.
out.other_title: Amplification by delegation to subquestions with supervised distillation
out.rationale: Christiano et al. instantiate amplification by delegation: H names subquestions, X answers them and H composes an answer. Wu et al. describe task decomposition: a human splits a parent task into simpler subtasks whose responses help a human provide a training signal, and the resulting dataset is used to train a model to perform two fundamental operations, the first being Decompose. The cited Wu et al. passage does not mention Christiano et al. or amplification, so the link records two parallel decomposition schemes for the same question rather than one building on the other.
out.scope: proposed SAME_QUESTION_DIFFERENT_SETTING: how a human can supervise a task by splitting it into simpler subquestions or subtasks; Christiano et al. use delegation to subquestions answered by X, while Wu et al. use a recursive tree of subtasks whose leaf tasks a human can demonstrate or evaluate

text: The authors define task decomposition as a human splitting a parent task into simpler subtasks whose responses would help a human provide a training signal for the parent, applied recursively so leaf tasks are simple enough for a human to demonstrate or evaluate. The resulting dataset can be used to train a model to perform two fundamental operations, the first being Decompose (ask for responses to a set of simpler tasks).
title: Task decomposition: tree of simpler subtasks that help a human supervise the parent
